summary:
Kuwait criminalised "imitating the opposite sex in any way" in 2007, when the National Assembly added Article 199 bis to Penal Code Article 198, punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine of 1,000 dinars (about US$3,500). Human Rights Watch reported that the only known targets of the provision were transgender people, who could neither change their legal documents nor find protection from such policing. Within two weeks of the law taking effect, at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, coffee shops and taxis; three were beaten, one into unconsciousness, and heads were shaved as punishment. HRW's 2012 report "They Hunt Us Down for Fun" documented police violence against trans women under the provision.

The 2007 amendment was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei and passed with overwhelming parliamentary support. In February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck it down as unconstitutional, after an individual targeted by police brought the challenge; the ruling is recorded by both Human Rights Watch and the Library of Congress. HRW urged the National Assembly to repeal the statute outright, observing that the judgment removed criminal exposure without ending the underlying dress-code policing practice. A cisgender woman arrested over a short haircut was later awarded 4,000 dinars in compensation, with the Court of Cassation finding that police had detained her "without justification." Being visibly trans is no longer a crime in Kuwait, and Kuwait is the only Gulf state to have repealed its cross-dressing statute.

Criminal exposure elsewhere in the penal code is unchanged. Article 193 still punishes consensual sexual relations between men by up to seven years, and adultery by up to five years. There is no route to changing gender markers on legal documents, so a visitor whose papers do not match their presentation has no domestic remedy for the mismatch.

Discrimination did not end with the ruling. Writing a year after the Constitutional Court decision, DAWN MENA reported that transgender people continue to face social and employment discrimination in practice, and that the judgment was not a first step toward recognition of transgender rights.

Regional conditions shape the risk. Gender segregation and enforced dress codes make trans people especially vulnerable across the area, according to Brian Whitaker's 2016 overview. Human Rights Watch's 2018 study of LGBT activism across 22 jurisdictions in the region, based on interviews with 34 activists, found that six interviewees from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or their activism.
tangentialFactors:
Censorship narrows access to information. The communications regulator CITRA blocked LGBTQI+ material, including advocacy content and legal information, according to the US State Department's 2023 country report; censors also banned the film "The Danish Girl" in Kuwait alongside other regional states. A visitor researching rights or support networks before or during travel may find those resources unreachable on local networks.

Political visibility is effectively absent. No candidate in the National Assembly election openly acknowledged an LGBTQI+ orientation, a finding from the same State Department report. The Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute's July 2024 analysis sets out the steps it considers still necessary after the abolition of the 2007 provision, indicating that the repeal settled the criminal-law question without delivering a wider framework of protection.

Kuwait's position relative to its neighbours is unusual rather than protective: it retains the region's general criminalisation of consensual same-sex relations while having removed the cross-dressing offence that its neighbours still hold on the books.
localsOnly:
Residents live with the practical consequences of a legal identity that cannot be corrected. Because gender markers on official documents cannot be changed, transgender Kuwaitis face a permanent mismatch between paperwork and presentation in employment, banking, and dealings with the security services.

DAWN MENA's February 2023 assessment, one year after the Constitutional Court ruling, records continuing social and employment discrimination against transgender people, and characterises the decision as an absence of criminal penalty rather than an advance in recognised rights.

Activism carries a cost measured in departure. In Human Rights Watch's 2018 regional study of LGBT activism, based on 34 interviews, six activists from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco had left for Europe because staying was unsafe for them.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the National Assembly has since enacted a replacement or amending statute after the Constitutional Court struck Article 198 is not resolved by the sources held here; HRW's February 2022 appeal for outright parliamentary repeal is the last word available on the legislative track.

Enforcement data after February 2022 is thin. The inventory contains no post-ruling arrest figures, so the frequency of dress-code stops, raids, or administrative harassment of transgender people since the ruling is not sourced and should be treated as unknown rather than as absent.

How Article 193 is applied in practice to transgender people, as distinct from cisgender men who have sex with men, is not documented in these sources; the seven-year penalty is stated for consensual relations between men without further specification.

The compensation award to the cisgender woman detained over a short haircut is carried from the existing record; the case number and the date of the Court of Cassation judgment are not verified against a primary source in this inventory.
